lead: Avionics means aviation electronics: every electronic system on an aircraft or spacecraft that senses, computes, communicates, navigates, controls or displays. An airliner, a fighter, a satellite and a small drone all use the same building blocks: sensors, computers, data buses, displays and controls, power and cooling. What changes is the priority. An airliner must be safe and on time, a fighter must win its mission and survive, a spacecraft must look after itself far from any repair, and a UAV must do its job on a few kilograms and a few hundred watts.

blocks.text: Aircraft electronics grew in four steps, each set by the parts available.

items: Valve era (1920s to 1950s): radios used vacuum tubes (valves). Instruments were mechanical or pneumatic, each standing alone.
Transistor era (1950s and 1960s): transistors made radios and autopilots smaller, cooler and more reliable; analog computers ran autopilots, and inertial navigation appeared on long-range aircraft.

Digital era (1970s and 1980s): microprocessors arrived, and digital data buses replaced bundles of wires: MIL-STD-1553 for military aircraft (first issued in 1973) and ARINC 429 for airliners. Screens began to replace dials in the early 1980s, and the Airbus A320 (1988) brought digital fly-by-wire to airliners.

Integrated era (1990s onward): functions began to share computers: the Boeing 777 (1995) used a shared cabinet, and the Airbus A380 (2007) and Boeing 787 (2011) use integrated modular avionics on switched Ethernet.

blocks.text: Military aircraft followed the same path, ending in systems that fuse radar, infrared and radio data into one picture.
One way to organise all of this is by function. Some syllabi call it the organisation framework of avionics:

items: Communication, navigation and surveillance (CNS): radios, navigation receivers, transponders and ADS-B.
Flight control and flight management: autopilot, fly-by-wire computers, flight management system.
Displays and crew interface: screens, head-up display, controls, warnings.
Aircraft systems management: engine, fuel, electrical, hydraulic and maintenance computers.
Mission systems (military and special-purpose aircraft): radar, electro-optical sensors, electronic warfare, weapons.

blocks.text: Civil avionics is designed for safety, regularity (on-time departures) and low cost of ownership. Certification is the main driver. Every failure condition is classified by its effect, and the more severe the effect, the less probable it must be. The usual targets for large aeroplanes are: catastrophic not more than 10⁻⁹ per flight hour (called extremely improbable), hazardous not more than 10⁻⁷, and major not more than 10⁻⁵. No single computer is that reliable, so civil designs use two or three independent channels that check each other.

Military avionics is designed for mission success and survivability. Its electronics meet high g, vibration, heat and jamming, and are built to military environmental and interference standards (MIL-STD-810 for environment, MIL-STD-461 for electromagnetic interference). Typical functions are radar, electronic warfare, electro-optical and infrared (EO/IR) sensors and stores management (control of weapons carriage and release). Redundancy here also means graceful degradation: a damaged aircraft keeps flying with fewer functions.
The word payload means what the platform carries to do its job. Payloads fall into a few types, and stores (weapons) are not sensors:

blocks.text: Spacecraft avionics is designed for autonomy. A satellite cannot be repaired, and the ground may hear it only during short passes. Radiation can flip a memory bit (a single-event upset) or slowly damage parts, so the on-board computer runs fault detection, isolation and recovery (FDIR): it spots a fault, switches to a spare unit and keeps the craft safe. The main blocks are on-board data handling, telemetry, tracking and command (TT&C) links, attitude and orbit control, and solar-array and battery power.

UAV avionics is designed for size, weight and power (SWaP). A small UAV carries an autopilot, GNSS and inertial sensors, a command-and-control (C2) datalink to the ground control station and a payload link. Every watt and gram comes out of endurance. The datalink can be lost, so the UAV must have a pre-planned lost-link behaviour (loiter, return home or land) and a geofence.

examples.question: A flight-control computer channel has a failure rate λ = 2 × 10⁻⁴ per flight hour. Loss of all channels is catastrophic, so the target is 10⁻⁹ per flight hour. Assume the channels fail independently and treat a one-hour flight. (a) Find the probability that one channel fails. (b) Find the probability that both channels of a duplex system fail. (c) Repeat for a triplex system. (d) Which layout meets the target?
steps: One channel: P₁ = 1 − e<sup>−λt</sup> with t = 1 h. Since λt = 2 × 10⁻⁴ is small, P₁ ≈ λt = 2 × 10⁻⁴ (the exact value is 1.9998 × 10⁻⁴).
Duplex: the system is lost only if both independent channels fail, so P₂ = P₁² = (2 × 10⁻⁴)² = 4 × 10⁻⁸.
Compare with 10⁻⁹: P₁ = 2 × 10⁻⁴ and P₂ = 4 × 10⁻⁸ are both larger, so they fail the target. P₃ = 8 × 10⁻¹² is smaller, so triplex passes with a factor of 10⁻⁹ ÷ (8 × 10⁻¹²) = 125 to spare.

Caution: this assumes independent failures. A common cause, such as the same software bug in all three channels or one shared power supply, defeats the squaring and cubing. That is why designers add dissimilar hardware or software and separate power.
examples.answer: Single channel 2 × 10⁻⁴, duplex 4 × 10⁻⁸, triplex 8 × 10⁻¹² per flight hour; only the triplex system meets the 10⁻⁹ target.

examples.question: A survey UAV has 2.0 kWh of usable battery energy. Propulsion takes 400 W, the autopilot 10 W, the datalink 30 W and the camera payload 60 W. (a) Find the endurance. (b) The designer adds two more autopilot channels of 10 W each for redundancy. Find the new endurance and the minutes lost.
steps: Time lost: 4.0 − 3.846 = 0.154 h = 0.154 × 60 = 9.2 minutes, before counting the extra mass of the two boxes.
examples.answer: Endurance falls from 4.0 h to 3.85 h, a loss of about 9.2 minutes per flight. On a UAV, redundancy is paid for in endurance, which is why UAV designs use fewer channels and careful lost-link behaviour.

traps: Calling ADS-B a navigation system. ADS-B Out broadcasts the aircraft's own position and identity for surveillance; the position comes from GNSS.
Listing weapons as sensors. Stores are a payload controlled by stores management; radar, EO/IR and SIGINT are the sensing payloads.
Squaring a failure probability without saying the channels must be independent. A common-mode fault makes the duplex system no better than one channel.
Treating UAV avionics as small airliner avionics. SWaP limits and datalink loss change the whole architecture.

quiz.q: Name the five functional groups of the avionics organisation framework.
quiz.a: Communication, navigation and surveillance; flight control and flight management; displays and crew interface; aircraft systems management; mission systems.

quiz.q: Why did transistors and then microprocessors change aircraft electronics?
quiz.a: Transistors replaced valves, so equipment became smaller, cooler and more reliable. Microprocessors let one box compute many functions in software and send results on a digital bus, which led to glass displays and integrated avionics.

quiz.q: Give the civil probability targets for catastrophic, hazardous and major failure conditions.
quiz.a: Catastrophic: not more than 10⁻⁹ per flight hour. Hazardous: not more than 10⁻⁷. Major: not more than 10⁻⁵.

quiz.q: A channel has λ = 5 × 10⁻⁵ per flight hour. Find the one-hour loss probability for duplex and triplex, and say which meets 10⁻⁹.
quiz.a: P₁ ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁵. Duplex: (5 × 10⁻⁵)² = 2.5 × 10⁻⁹, just above the target, so it fails. Triplex: 1.25 × 10⁻¹³, which passes.

quiz.q: A UAV has 1.5 kWh usable and draws 300 W. A new payload adds 75 W. Find the endurance before and after.
quiz.a: Before: 1500 ÷ 300 = 5.0 h. After: 1500 ÷ 375 = 4.0 h. The payload costs one hour.

quiz.q: Compare the redundancy philosophy of an airliner, a fighter and a satellite.
quiz.a: Airliner: two or three identical or dissimilar channels so that a failure leaves full function and the aircraft can be dispatched. Fighter: graceful degradation after damage, accepting reduced mission capability. Satellite: cold or warm spares switched in by FDIR, because no repair is possible and the ground is rarely in contact.

beyond: Not for the exam. Military programmes now push open mission systems, where new sensors and software can be added without redesigning the aircraft. Spacecraft use radiation-tolerant processors and software that recovers from upsets by itself. Larger UAVs are working towards certified detect-and-avoid so that they can fly in normal airspace. Search for 'open mission systems', 'FDIR spacecraft', 'detect and avoid' and 'SWaP-C'.

spec.aria: Three rows: simplex with one channel box, duplex with two, triplex with three. Each row has a bar on a log scale of the probability of losing every channel in a one-hour flight: 2 times 10 to the minus 4, 4 times 10 to the minus 8, and 8 times 10 to the minus 12. A dashed line marks the civil target of 10 to the minus 9. The first two bars cross it and fail; the triplex bar stays left of it and meets the target.
